Mydeimos reached up to cup his cheek, guiding his gaze down. “You never do.”

And then his other hand slipped to the hem of Phainon’s tunic, tugging gently. An invitation. No urgency. Just undeniable trust.

Phainon’s mouth found his again, slower this time, lips parting with heat and wonder. Every touch, every breath, felt deeper. Less about desire, more about devotion. It was intimacy that didn’t need to be chased. It simply existed, growing fuller between them.

Clothes loosened, discarded in a scatter of silk and linen across the pillows. Skin met skin, warm and flushed, the soft friction of shared heat and whispered names. Mydeimos was given the complete control. His body moving on top of Phainon’s as naturally as the tide drew back the shore, steady and sure.

His fingers raked through Phainon’s silvery hair, drawing him closer. Their mouths met again, then parted, then met once more, as if they were relearning each other with each breath.

Phainon’s lips brushed against Mydeimos' pulse. His thumb stroked the underside of his wrist, matching the rhythm. “I love you,” he murmured. “I love you more than I can bear.”

Mydeimos didn’t reply, not with words. But with how his body guided them to the peak. His moves grew a bit faster. His eyes, when they fluttered open, said everything.

And later, as the moon crept past the window, casting light onto their shared silhouette, the room calmed down again. Phainon held Mydeimos against his chest, their fingers still laced over the firm curve of the life between them. There was nothing more to say.

Only the hush of breath, the warmth of skin, and the confession already carved into the space between each heartbeat.

**

chapters.title: And Then There were Three
chapters.html:
The library was too big for just two people. Sunlight filtered through tall, ancient windows and dust hovered lazily in the air, disturbed only when Cyrene yanked another leather-bound tome from the overstuffed shelf with a huff.

“How many languages are you even allowed to name a child in?” she muttered, flipping a page with disdain. “Half these names sound like battle cries. Or funeral rites.”

Phainon, curled up awkwardly on a velvet chaise with several volumes piled beside him. “You’re in Kremnos. Everything here either sounds like a curse or a prophecy.”

“Or both,” Cyrene sniffed, holding a particularly ominous title aloft. ‘The Lineage of Bloody Lion.’ “Do you think this one comes with a free haunting?”

"Fret not, Ptolemy said most of the books here are purified."

"Most, right?" Cyrene winced and returned the book into the shelves.

Phainon grinned, eyes trailing over a list of old names. “I could name him after a flower,” he mused aloud.

"Only if it’s a flower that could kill a man.”

Phainon raised a brow. “You're mocking my aesthetics.”

“I’m protecting the child’s future.” She waved a hand. “You can’t give a future heir a name like Blossom.”

“Fine,” he sighed, flipping another page. “What about something regal? Like Aventurine for a man? Or Herta for a girl?”

Cyrene shook her head. “Aventurine sounds like someone who cheats at dice and Herta sounds like a narcissistic lady.”

Phainon groaned, tossing the book onto the growing pile of rejects. “This is impossible. Everything sounds like a big no.”

“Or weird,” she added helpfully.

“Or belong to unanimated object.”

She paused, narrowing her eyes. “Please tell me you weren’t considering naming your child 'Meropide'.”

Phainon looked too guilty.

“No.”

“It has a nice sound!”

“It’s a name of prison, Phai.”

“Fine,” he muttered, falling back dramatically onto the chaise, arms flopped outward. “My child will be nameless. That’s the decision. They shall be the Nameless Royal IX.”

"Why IX?"

"No reason. Just a random number to make them sounded like a royalty."

“The king told me to make sure you didn’t  choose anything too absurd so, rejected.” Cyrene leaned back on her heels, idly stacking books. “Or you could just do what every other overwhelmed parent does and name him after someone you love.”

Phainon didn’t reply.

Cyrene blinked, catching the stillness in the air. When she turned, she saw him looking down at his lap, one hand resting thoughtfully over the cover of an old genealogy scroll. His mouth had softened into a quiet smile, small, almost boyish. One of those rare moments where Phainon looked more like the dreamy younger brother she used to boss around, and less like a man soon to be father to a future monarch.

“You already chose, didn’t you?” she asked, gentler now.

He nodded.

Cyrene crossed her arms, waiting.

But Phainon simply picked up a pen and scribbled the name into the edge of a folded parchment, tucking it into the front of his tunic.

“Not telling?”

“Not yet,” he said, still smiling. “Mydei will hear it first.”

Cyrene smirked. “Fair enough. But if it ends up being Blossom, I’m still throwing a shoe at you.”

“Noted.”

The royal chamber had never felt this quiet.

Phainon stood beside the bed, hands clasped tightly around Mydei’s. His palms were damp, either from sweat or from the sheer heat pulsing through his skin. He couldn’t tell. All he knew was that his husband's fingers still curled around his own.

On the bed, Mydeimos lay reclined against the propped cushions, his breath steady, eyes half-lidded but sharp. The bump of his belly rose under the thin silk robe he wore, cradled by gentle folds of cloth. The curve of impending life was stark now, pressing outward like a quiet miracle carved into his frame.

“You’re trembling,” Mydeimos said softly, his golden eyes never leaving Phainon’s face.

Phainon forced a smile, strained and fleeting. “I’m not.”

“You are.”

He opened his mouth to argue, but the words caught behind his teeth, tangled in emotion too vast to name. Eventually, he bowed his head, resting their joined hands against his brow. Mydei’s skin was warm. Alive. So alive.

“It will be okay,” Mydeimos murmured, calm and gentle like morning light breaking across a stormed sea. “You need to breathe.”

“I am breathing,” Phainon mumbled, but the shakiness in his exhale betrayed him. “This is Perdikkas’ first time doing this,” he added, more urgently, more vulnerable than before. “He’s never—this is different from stitching wounds or setting bones. They will...”

“—cut me open,” Mydeimos finished with a smile. “It's fine. Perdikkas might be new but his assistants are veteran. Although not for a man, they handled surgery for women before.”

“Dei—” Phainon’s voice cracked, and he squeezed his husband’s hand tighter. “That doesn’t bother you? You'll be in pain.”

“I’ve had worse wounds,” Mydeimos said, without flinching. “Remember the ambush at Northwest Pass? Or when the poisoned blade hit my rib? This—” he paused, glancing down to the swell of his stomach, “—this will be nothing like those. Because this wound isn’t from hate. It’s not meant to kill. This is for our child, Phainon. That’s all we need to know.”

Phainon looked at him like he was seeing him anew. Braver than any war-blooded general, gentler than the wise hermit.

“I know,” he whispered. “I know, it’s just... if anything happens to you—”

“It won’t.”

Phainon’s lips thinned, but he nodded, the knot in his chest only half-loosened.

Just then, the door opened with a polite knock that barely masked the tension humming beyond it. Perdikkas entered, robes neatly tied, gloves already prepared. Behind him stood the midwife, older and calm, her face lined with a wisdom. They both bowed at the royal couple, and Perdikkas didn’t waste time.

“The room is ready,” he said gently, not to rush, but to prepare. “We’ll begin soon. It’s time to move, Your Majesty.”

Mydeimos gave a nod. He didn’t flinch. “Understood.”

Then, he turned back to Phainon and smiled, one hand still tucked in his. “See you later?”

Phainon blinked fast. That casual question, so light and familiar, punched the air from his lungs.

“See you later,” he echoed. His voice was barely a murmur.

He bent down. First pressing his lips against Mydei’s forehead, then the soft skin beneath his right eye. A kiss to the left lid, then to the bridge of his nose. Then each cheek, warm and flushed. Finally, gently, reverently, he brushed his mouth over the lips. It wasn’t deep. It wasn’t rushed. It held the weight of every promise he'd ever made.

“I’ll be right outside,” he whispered against his skin. “The whole time.”

Mydeimos' eyes fluttered shut for a moment, nodding wordlessly.

And then the aides arrived with the moving cot. Soft instructions followed, careful as a ritual. Phainon stepped aside, only just, as they gently helped the king to shift and settle onto the rolling bed. Phainon’s hand never left Mydeimos' until the last possible second, fingers slipping apart only when they had no choice.

He stood there, breath caught in his throat, as the doors opened and his dearest was slowly wheeled out, surrounded by quiet footsteps and hushed tension.

The sun filtering through the windows was pale, as though the world itself held its breath. Phainon too didn’t move until Mydeimos disappeared from view.

And even then, he stayed standing there a moment longer, eyes fixed on the space his husband had just occupied, one hand still hovering mid-air, aching with the absence.

Phainon didn’t wait alone.

From the moment Mydeimos left for the surgery, Phainon’s world had narrowed. But Caelus and Dan Heng were already there. The first was leaning against the pillar with crossed arms and a restless tap of his foot, the other sitting nearby, silent but steady, like a watchtower against storm. Audata offered to help with preparing the royal chamber so she left first although Phainon knew his mother was just trying to keep herself busy, couldn't stay still without feeling anxious.

Nonetheless, the hallway wasn’t empty. Servants moved quietly past, and guards kept their distance. Still, the space around Phainon felt hollow. Echoing. It rang with the silence of a heart not yet heard.

Caelus tried to distract him with soft jokes, half-baked humor. Dan Heng offered reassurances, gentle and measured. Phainon responded with nods, faint smiles, small words but the longer he waited, the more those gestures frayed.

Time moved like smoke. No clocks, no bells. Just the steady rhythm of fear pressing tighter against his ribs.

Then it happened. A sound from within.

A cry.

One, loud and fierce, enough to shatter the tension in the air.

Phainon bolted upright from the bench he hadn’t even realized he sat on. He turned toward the chamber door, blinking fast. His lips parted as the sound echoed again, thin, helpless, alive.

A baby’s cry.

Their baby.

Phainon’s chest caved in with relief. A breath escaped him, ragged and trembling with joy. He nearly collapsed back against the wall as Caelus whooped beside him, clapping him on the back.

“It's here,” Caelus grinned. “That’s your kid!”

Dan Heng’s lips quirked upward, and for a moment, Phainon could feel the tide of panic beginning to retreat.

But then Perdikkas burst through the chamber door.

His gloves were bloody. Not just stained, soaked. There was no serenity in his face, no joy in the lines of his jaw. Just haste.

“My queen,” he said, “Your child... The royal prince is born. Healthy.”

Phainon tried to speak, but nothing came out but a stunned grin. He nodded, tears stinging at the corners of his eyes.

But Perdikkas wasn’t done. He turned sharply, called out behind him,  “Peucesta! Leonnius! Hurry!”

The two aides, stationed nearby, bolted forward without question. They entered the chamber in silence, the door thudding shut behind them again.

Phainon’s smile faltered. His heart, still caught in the joy of hearing his child, now dropped like a stone.

( That wasn’t right. )

His lungs squeezed. He took a step forward, uncertain, as though his legs might betray him.

Caelus blinked. “Huh? What happened?”

Dan Heng straightened beside him.

Phainon shook his head. “No. No.”


He ran to the door, almost touched the handle, then froze. He wasn’t allowed in.


Not yet.


He looked back at Caelus and Dan Heng. “That’s not normal, right? Calling in more aides? That’s not—”


Neither responded.


The quiet was a noose around his throat.


“Say something!” Phainon snapped. “Tell me it’s fine. Tell me he’s fine.”


Caelus opened his mouth. Closed it again. 


Dan Heng was the one who tried to smooth the tension. “If it was urgent, you’d be told.”


Phainon scoffed softly under his breath. “Unless they’re too busy trying to keep him alive to say anything.”


The joy he’d felt minutes ago turned bitter in his throat. He staggered back from the door and leaned against the cold stone wall, one hand over his mouth as if to keep himself from breaking apart.


He whispered Mydei’s name like a prayer. Over and over.


Mydei, who always bled quietly. Mydei, who never let anyone see the wounds. Mydei, who smiled even when it hurt. Mydei, who went willingly into this pain for them.


“What if he’s—what if he’s bleeding too much?” Phainon croaked. “What if something tore—what if they’re trying to fix it and can’t?”


His knees gave in. He sank down, pressing his palms to his forehead, breathing too fast.


Caelus dropped beside him, arm over his shoulders. “He’s strong, Phai. He's immortal, remember?"


“That doesn’t mean he’s immune to pain?! There might be something that can turn him mortal too. Mydei told me one and what if there's more weakness to it that we are not aware of...” Phainon’s voice cracked, low and hoarse.


Dan Heng sat across from him, hands folded in his lap. “But he’s not alone in there. Let's trust them.”


Phainon shook his head, tears burning behind his eyes, refusing to fall.


“I should’ve been in there,” he whispered. “He shouldn’t be alone. I should’ve—”


“He wouldn’t want you see him in pain,” Caelus interrupted, gently. “You know that.”


Phainon gripped the edge of the bench beside him, white-knuckled. His chest ached. Not from the waiting but from the memories.


The way Mydei had smiled before being wheeled away.


See you later, he’d said.


It rang now like a farewell.


“No,” Phainon muttered. “You promised, Mydei. You said you’d see me again. We need to make that family portrait, remembere?” Phainon pressed his palm to his chest, where his heart beat wild and uneven.


“Come back,” he whispered under his breath. “Please, Mydei. I need you... Your child needs you...”


Phainon covered his face, starting to chant his name like prayers, hoping that any benevolent titan out there would grant his wish.


"Please, come back to us, Mydei..."


The doors opened at last.


Phainon shot to his feet before the creak had fully echoed. His heart slammed against his ribs, only to falter when Perdikkas stepped out.


No blood on his gloves this time.


Just a hand raised in calm and a weary, warm smile on his face.


“It’s done,” Perdikkas said softly, placing a firm hand on Phainon’s shoulder. “The operation was successful. Your child is safe… and so is our King.”


It was only then—only after hearing it aloud—that Phainon felt the tension drain from his body.


And then he collapsed.


His knees gave out, his legs folding under him like parchment caught in rain, and he hit the stone floor with a choked sob. He covered his face with both hands, shoulders trembling as the tears rushed out, hot and unashamed. He wept without holding back. Fear had eaten him alive for hours and he could finally spat back out.


“Thank you,” he gasped, breaking around the words. “Thank you. Oh, Titans, thank you.”


Perdikkas crouched beside him and squeezed his shoulder. “Mydeimos is still unconscious, but it’s only natural. He’ll wake. Give him a little time.”


Phainon nodded, still trembling, wiping at his face with the heel of his palm.


“You should see your son,” Perdikkas added. “Hephaestion’s had the maid clean him. He’s in the next room.”


Phainon turned his head toward the nursery door, breath catching. His son.


His son.


He swallowed hard, pushed himself to his feet, and turned to Caelus and Dan Heng, who had waited with him through it all, who had said nothing but offered their presence.


“I... thank you,” Phainon murmured hoarsely. “For staying.”


Caelus grinned, uncharacteristically soft. “We’ll be here when you come out, Dad.”


Dan Heng nodded, eyes steady. “Go meet him.”


With that, Phainon followed Perdikkas to the next chamber. The hallway seemed quieter now, the air softer. As if the castle itself had exhaled. As if it, too, had been holding its breath.


The nursery was small, warmly lit. Hephaestion was there, speaking in low tones to the maids before stepping back with a nod of greeting. At the center of the room was a cradle, carved from pale wood and etched with gentle sun motifs. And inside—


Phainon moved forward slowly.


Tiny.


Swaddled in soft cloth, a baby lay asleep, chest rising and falling with peaceful rhythm. The moment Phainon drew near, the light caught his hair, silvery-blue strands, impossibly soft and already curling a little at the crown.


His knees nearly buckled again.


He reached down, hands trembling, and gathered the child into his arms. The weight was small, warm. Real. The baby shifted slightly at the touch, let out a little sigh, and then, blinking against the light, opened his eyes.


Golden.


A golden so clear and familiar it robbed Phainon’s breath.


“Mydei...” he whispered, as though the name alone could describe the color. “You’ve got his pretty eyes. How lucky.”


The baby wriggled in his arms, and Phainon instinctively adjusted his hold, swaying gently as if he’d done this a hundred times. His thumb brushed the soft cheek. The baby blinked again, then let out a short yawn before settling once more.


“You’re beautiful,” Phainon said quietly. “Just like your father. So pretty."


There was no need to wonder who he looked like. He looked like both of them. The silver of Phainon’s hair. The firelight gold of Mydemos' gaze. Their son.


Still cradling him, Phainon lowered himself onto the chair by the window. He sat in silence for a long time, just rocking gently, memorizing the weight, the warmth, the miracle in his arms.


He wanted Mydeimos to see their son too. To hold him. To know that everything they had endured—every risk, every fear, every scar—had led to this.


To this child.


To this family.


He smiled, tears falling again, but they were more from joy now.


“You’ve got the best father. A king, a very beautiful, cool and dependable king,” Phainon whispered to the baby. “And I’m going to be everything you need. I swear it. Just like I promised him, I promise you. I'll built a gentle space for three of us.”


The baby’s hand curled near his collar.


Phainon kissed the tiny knuckle, then rested his cheek against the crown of his son’s head.


Outside the nursery window, the wind stirred gently through the courtyard trees, carrying the hush of twilight and the beginning which no longer carried dread.

Mydeimos walked slowly, as if he feared waking from something not quite real. The petals crunched softly beneath his bare feet, pale blossoms scattered like snow along the winding path. The air was warm, humming faintly with birdsong and the perfume of wildflowers. It smelled like childhood. Like the old garden before it was razed.


At the end of the path, a bungalow stood quietly beside a still lake, its roof dappled with vines, windows wide open to the breeze. A figure stood by the porch, turned slightly away. Golden eyes. Blond hair, long and braided over one shoulder. Her frame was lean, familiar, uncannily so. The same slope of nose. The same quiet strength in her posture. Yet she wore it with softness.


His breath caught.


“...Mother?”


The woman turned. Her smile unfurled like the first light of morning, warm and boundless. Mydeimos hadn’t seen that smile in over than a decade, but the warmth of it hit him like a wave. She then opened her arms, welcoming.


He ran.


He stumbled a little in his haste, almost tripping over the edge of a root, but he didn’t care. He fell into her embrace as though he had never left it. His fingers clawed into the back of her tunic, trembling, desperate. 


“I missed you,” he gasped, the words cracking open from his chest. “I missed you so much.”

And then the tears came. He didn’t try to stop them. Quiet at first, then wracked, like the sound had waited years to break loose.


“I’m sorry. I’m so sorry. I couldn’t do anything. I wasn’t strong enough. I couldn’t save you. I ran too late, and because of me, you...”


“Hush,” she murmured, low and steady, fingers threading through his hair like she used to when he was small and scared. “You were a child. It was never your burden.”


“I should’ve tried harder!”


“You survived, Mydeimos.” She pulled back to hold his face between her palms. “That was all I ever wanted. That was everything.”


His breath trembled. His eyes were red. “I wanted to save you.”


She kissed his forehead gently. “And I wanted to save you. You’re living well. And that’s enough. Come, let's talk.”


Gorgo led him to sit down on the patch of grass by the lake, shoulder to shoulder. She took off her shoes and dipped her feet into the water with a content sigh. Mydeimos followed, watching the ripples dance around their ankles.


“You’ve grown,” she said after a moment, glancing sideways. “That braid suits you.”


He laughed, a little watery. “Didn’t have a choice. I’m a king now, apparently.”


“I see..."


He exhaled, softer. “It’s not what I wanted. But... it became something I know I have to do. We’re changing Kremnos. Bit by bit.”


He told her everything. About his advisors and friends, how they helped him remember who he was underneath the crown. How they laughed with him, scolded him, followed him into storms. About the reforms he’d managed to push through. The guilds. The council. The amnesty offered to the border rebels. The laws updated. The throne no longer being a cage.


Gorgo listened without interrupting. Her fingers twitched when he spoke of kindness. Her eyes softened when he named each friend with faint exasperation and unmistakable affection.


“And you?” she finally asked, resting her head lightly on his shoulder. “What about you, Mydei? What makes you smile now?”


He hesitated, then looked away.


“...There’s someone.”


Gorgo perked. “Oh?”


“My husband. Phainon. He’s…” Mydei exhaled. “Reckless. Sometimes I want to strangle him. But he’s the only one who ever looked at me like I wasn’t made of stone. Like I was allowed to be human.”


Gorgo hummed. “You sound like you adore him quite a lot.”


He blushed, eyes narrowing. “I do. It’s embarrassing.”


“That's good.”


He smiled, then looked down. His voice grew quieter. “...I underwent the rite. Changed my body. It hurt, excruciatingly. It was more painful than anything I’ve ever endured in war. It was like being shattered and being rebuilt while being wide awake. I could feel every part of me was twisted in a way it shouldn't be done.”


“You let yourself be broken just to build a future,” she murmured. “That’s how I know you’re mine.”


Mydeimos smiled gently. "I guess so. Well, Phainon didn't know though. I said it was fine. I didn't want him to get worried."


"Mydei, my dear," Gorgo cupped Mydei's cheek, "while I can see your reason, you should lean a bit more to your husband. Love comes with concern, that is inseparable. You can't always treat him like he is a fragile glass."


"I know, but..." He sighed. "I just don't want to cloud the sun..."


"The sun might disappear altogether if something happened when it could be prevented if only you let him know firsthand."


Mydei fell silence, let the words sunk into him. Part of him always knew about that and having his own mother spelt it directly made his mind strangely clearer.

"You, are right. I will try to be honest."

"Good," Gorgo stroked Mydeimos' cheek, gently, "Don't give a space for a regret that you can easily dodge..."

"Okay..." Mydeimos closed his eyes, felt the warmth of his mother's palm.


Changing the topic, Gorgo lowered her hand and touched Mydei's stomach. "The rite, it's successful, right?"


"Yeah..." That made Mydei remembered. He was in the middle of delivery before he came here. Panic was started to plague his mind.


"No, you're fine." As if reading his thought, Gorgo answered. "I just missed you so I took the chance for a little talk."


"I, see..." Mydei nodded, holding his mother's hand again.


"Tell me more about your husband."


"He is, well... He is amazing but somehow, he often looked down on himself. He panicked a lot. You should’ve seen his face when I told him I was carrying his child. He’s gotten worse since. Won’t let me do anything alone. Keeps tracking how much water I drink. Won’t stop massaging my feet.”


Gorgo hummed, amused. “Sounds like a good husband.”


“He is,” Mydei admitted. “His parents are kind, too. His mother fusses over me. His father dotes me a little too much by sending their harvests every time.”


“I’m glad,” Gorgo said, softly. “Glad you’ve found a life that holds you gently. Glad you’re safe. And loved.”


Mydei’s chest tightened. “But I wasn’t enough to keep you safe.”


“Stop,” she whispered. Her fingers turned his face toward hers. “Mydei. Listen to me. I did what I chose. I knew the cost. If we turned back the time, I'd make the same choice. You’ve lived, and that’s all I ever wanted. That is enough.”


He nodded, jaw clenched. She leaned forward and kissed his brow.


“Still, I'm sorry,” she said. “For leaving you so young. For not being there when you needed me.”


"No, Mother..." Mydei shook his head. "You're the reason why I am here, why I can change, why I believe Kremnos can change as well."


Gorgo smiled, nodding her head solemnly.


“Then stop carrying guilt that no longer belongs to you.”


He swallowed hard.


“You lived,” she whispered. “You endured. You made something better than what you came from. That is more than I ever dared hope.”


His lip quivered. “I just wanted you to see it. To know I didn’t waste what you gave me.”


“I see it,” she said, pressing her forehead to his. “And I am proud. Of the man you became. Of the boy who survived. Of the heart that still loves.”


He breathed out softly. “I still miss you.”


“I know.” She cupped his face again. “But I’m always with you. In the way you speak. In the way you hold your child. In the way you learned to choose love, even after loss.”


"...And I wish I could introduce Phainon to you."


"You already did. And I like him." She poked Mydei's nose. "After all, he makes you smile again."


They sat there as the sunlight deepened, the lake catching the gold of the sky.


But eventually, the path began to call him again.


She walked him to the bend in the trail. Held his hand to her cheek one last time.


“Will I see you again?”


Her smile was soft and steady.


“Whenever you need me,” she said. “Close your eyes, and I’ll be there. In the quiet. In the stillness. In the sound of your child laughing. I’m always close.”


He reached forward and kissed her forehead. Her hands lingered on his shoulders for a moment longer, as if reluctant to let him go.


“I love you,” he said.


“I never stopped,” she answered.


Then she let go.


He walked forward and looked behind one last time. But she was already gone, folded back into the bloom of myrtles.


He turned again, slowly walking back down the flowered path, the blossoms parting around him like waves. The light grew stronger with every step, gold and white, soft as breath. When it engulfed him, he squeezed his eyes shut.


And when he opened them again, there was warmth in his palm.


A hand, calloused and trembling faintly, clutching his own. Phainon. Curled beside the bed, still in his clothes, face drawn with exhaustion, like he hadn’t moved in hours.


Mydeimos blinked slowly. The room was dim, save for the afternoon light filtering through the curtains.


He shifted his fingers.


Phainon stirred instantly, gasping, eyes wide as he jolted upright.


“Mydei?”


A smile ghosted across Mydei’s lips.


“Hey.” he whispered.


Phainon exhaled a sob, forehead pressing to his knuckles.


“Welcome back, Mydei."


Mydeimos reached out with his free hand, brushing hair from Phainon’s brow.


“I'm sorry to make you wait."


"It's okay, as long as you come back to us." Phainon murmured, kissed Mydeimos' hand several times.


"Of course. I'll always come back to your side."


And this time, he meant it with everything that still beat in his chest.


When they finally brought the baby to him, Mydei was already sitting up, back against the pillow, eyes still faintly glazed from exhaustion.


Phainon held the bundle carefully, as if afraid the fragile miracle in his arms would disappear. His steps were soundless across the polished floor, breath was shallow. He didn’t even know he was crying again until the warmth of the tears blurred the baby’s soft features.


“Here,” he whispered.


Mydeimos reached out, steady, calm. The way he always was. Even the weight of an entire nation couldn’t shake the stoicism in his core. But when he held their child for the first time, that quiet composure softened into something else. Something raw, deeper affection, with a gentle curve of smile.


He chuckled.


“What?”


“Nine months carrying him in me, but this child chose to be your twin,” Mydeimos said, golden eyes fixed on the small face nestled in the crook of his arm. “Same nose. Same mouth. Same furrow between the brows when he sleeps.”


“Except the eyes,” Phainon murmured, dropping beside him. "He has yours."


“Hmm,” Mydeimos traced the baby's tiny cheek with a thumb. "Then I suppose I'll be content with that."


Silence curled around them, warm and slow, interrupted only by the soft snuffle of the newborn's breath. Then Mydei glanced sideways.


“Do you finally have a name in mind?”


"Haha, after weeks of looking through various books, I made up my mind." Phainon hesitated, then nodded. “I’d like to name him Khaslana.”


Mydei paused. For a heartbeat, the air stilled completely.


“Khaslana?” he echoed, gentler now.


Phainon’s smile wavered, lips trembling with the weight of it. “It was the name I always imagined for the kind of child I thought I’d never have. Strong. Bright. Someone who’d be loved right from the start.”


There was no mocking smile from Mydeimos this time. Just a soft exhale as he looked down again, the name settling between them like a seed in fertile ground.


“Khaslana,” he repeated. “He’ll be loved, Phainon.”


At that, Phainon’s chest rose sharply then crumpled. The tears returned without permission, and he pressed a shaking hand over his mouth to stifle a quiet sob. It wasn’t sorrow. It wasn’t fear. Just overwhelming everything. To see Mydei, alive, safe, and now cradling the tiny life they made together was more than his heart could hold.


“You’re crying again,” Mydeimos sighed, though there was no real irritation in his voice.


“I can't help it...” Phainon sniffled.


“Crybaby.”


“Well, you need to stop being so perfect about everything. It’s your fault.”


Mydei rolled his eyes. “Lower your voice. You’ll wake—”


Before he could finish, the baby shifted. Tiny fists flexed. A sharp little cry rang out, mewling and impatient. Mydei sighed and shifted his robe aside, baring his chest with ease as he guided the infant to latch. It wasn't so flawless but he tried his best to adjust, to make it easier for his baby.


Phainon’s breath caught again, but this time it ended in a soft laugh. The sight was just so tender that it squeezed his heart warmly.


“I have to share your chest now, huh?” he said, wiping his face with the heel of his hand. “Tsk. You’re spoiling him early.”


Mydei narrowed his eyes. “You’re lucky I’m too occupied to throw something at you.”


“You’re literally feeding our child right now. That’s the most powerful comeback you could possibly have.”


The baby suckled quietly, the room falling into a hush again. Only this time it was a hush filled with warmth, with the closeness of new life and old love, of vows that meant more than ceremony and a family that wasn’t built by duty but by choice.


Phainon leaned in, brushing his lips against Mydei’s temple. His hand gently stroked the baby’s back where it rested against Mydei’s chest.


Khaslana. Golden-eyed and silvery-haired. A name carried from dream to breath to life.


And now, he became the new beginning of everything else.


**

chapters.title: In This Gentle World We Built
chapters.html:
They had survived wars, revolutions, conspiracies, ancient rites. But no battlefield, not even the blood-soaked courts of Kremnos, could prepare them for the siege of parenthood.


It began the very first night.


Khaslana, barely a day old, had lungs like an emergency alarm. Phainon was the first to leap from the bed when the wailing began, fumbling in the half-light to lift their son from the cradle.


“I think he’s hungry,” he whispered, eyes already glassy with panic.


“I just fed him an hour ago,” Mydei murmured into the pillow, his tone was laced with fatigue.


“He got your determination,” Phainon said.


“No, he got your insatiable hunger.”


Still, Mydei sat up, wordlessly shifting his robe and reaching for the child. The moment Khaslana latched, the room was quiet again, except for the soft, rhythmic sucking.


They fell into a rhythm over the days that followed. Or rather, tried to.


Phainon insisted on taking the late shift. He would hold Khaslana, walk with him, even hum lullabies off-key in the dark. But no matter how carefully he swayed or how securely he bundled the baby, Khaslana seemed to have a sixth sense that Mydei wasn’t nearby. The cries would start again soon enough, sharp and persistent, until Mydei sat up with a groan.


Again and again.


One night, Mydei had just managed to doze off, cheek pressed to Phainon’s shoulder, a hand still resting on the edge of the crib, when Khaslana wailed. Phainon moved first, bleary-eyed and sighing. While Mydei mumbled, “I swear if he’s just crying because I exhaled too loud...”


“He’s sensitive. Like his father,” Phainon said as he picked up the baby.


"You meant yourself, right?" Phainon grinned, shrugging nonchalantly.


By the end of the second week, they were shadows of themselves. Still beautiful, still in love, but with hair out of place and eye bags so deep they could’ve stored winter grains. Mydei once walked into a council meeting wearing mismatched shoes and didn’t notice until Leonnius whispered it across the room.


There were small mercies. Afternoon naps when Khaslana finally slept long enough for both of them to collapse. A warm meal brought up by Audata. A kiss on the temple as they passed each other in the night, one holding the baby, the other fetching water, or ointment, or the fourth cloth of the evening.


And still, they adapted.


Phainon once learned how to change a cloth diaper using only one hand because the other was holding a scroll Mydei needed to review. Mydei perfected the art of breastfeeding while dictating letters. One morning, when Khaslana had finally fallen asleep, Mydei sagged into a chair, head tilted back, hair loose and eyes half-lidded.


“Sleep,” Phainon urged.


“I’m afraid if I close my eyes, I’ll open them and he’ll be ten.”


Phainon leaned down, kissed his forehead. “I'll be here to wake you up, don't worry.”


It wasn’t easy. It was never easy. But the moments in between, the quiet gurgles when Khaslana smiled in his sleep, the way he wrapped his tiny fingers around theirs made even the bone-deep exhaustion worth it.


And sometimes, in the softest hush of night, Mydei would wake only to find Phainon had beaten him to it, rocking Khaslana by the window, singing something low under his breath.


“I thought it was my turn,” Mydei would murmur.


“It’s always your turn,” Phainon whispered, smiling faintly. “But sometimes I want to steal it, just to give you a bit more sleep at least until he got tired with me and miss your warmth.”


Then Mydei would sit on the bed, watching his husband and his son, the light of the moon weaving between them, thinking nothing in the world could match this luminous ache of affection.


Time passed, not with wars but with toys left under the chairs and milk stains on royal robes.


Khaslana, now round-cheeked and toddling, had turned the palace into his playground. He walked with the steadiness of a drunken man, wobbling, planting his feet wide, arms flailing for balance. But each unsteady step was greeted with applause. Especially from Phainon, who trailed him with arms outstretched and voice rising mid-panic every time Khaslana veered near furniture.


“Watch out—ah, no, no, no, not the scroll shelf!” he cried once, just before the toddler successfully yanked a rolled treaty from a low rack. The scroll unraveled dramatically like a proud conquest, and Khaslana laughed at it as if he’d solved national policy.


“He’s going to lead a revolution by accident,” Mydei murmured dryly from his seat nearby, sipping tea.

"Please don't make my child sounds like a tyrant..."


At the same time, Phainon was fighting a more personal battle once he insisted he would handle Khaslana by his own than hiring a maid.


Now, Khaslana had entered the glorious stage of testing food. Which meant chewing was optional. Swallowing? Rare. But spitting? That was everywhere.


Each mealtime had become a gamble between fatherly optimism and soul-crushing despair.


Phainon knelt in front of the highchair with a spoonful of lovingly mashed carrots. “Okay, little warrior. This time, you’re going to eat this, and we’ll cheer, and Papa won’t cry in the courtyard again. Deal?”


Khaslana looked him straight in the eyes and with a grin, slowly opened his mouth.


Victory. Phainon dared to hope. He placed the spoon gently in.


There was one brief moment of blessed silence but then pfft, Bright orange mush landed on Phainon’s face, streaking across his cheek and his dignity.


He dropped the spoon. “He spat it. Again.”


Mydei, holding a towel and barely holding in a laugh, walked over to clean him. “He doesn’t like carrots. Maybe it’s revenge for the eggplant incident last week.”


“He liked the eggplant for two bites! I saw joy in his eyes!”


“He puked after that.”


"Right... But seriously, what is so hard from eating? He gonna give me gray hair soon." Phainon muttered, wiping his face as Khaslana giggled at his own culinary crime.


But, Phainon's struggle didn't end at food flinging and sleep-deprived negotiations.


One soft afternoon, sunlight spilling through the open window and Mydei resting cross-legged on a plush mat with Khaslana in his lap, something shifted.


Khaslana had been babbling for weeks now, gibberish with the occasional “ba” or “mam” thrown in, but nothing solid. Phainon had been working on it, though. Every night. Every walk. Every nap he whispered the same syllables in exaggerated, hopeful repetition.


“Say it with me: Pa-paaaa. Paaa...Paaa!”


But today, it happened out of nowhere.


Khaslana, golden-eyed and smug with toddler pride, reached his chubby arms up toward Mydei, leaned forward, and chirped, clear as day:


“Dada!”


Phainon dropped the basket of laundry he was folding.


Mydei blinked. “Did he just...?”


“NO,” Phainon howled, storming over with betrayal written across his face. “No! That is not the word we agreed on!”


Mydei was already scooping Khaslana closer, laughing in disbelief as the baby repeated, louder this time, “Dada!”


“Did you teach him that behind my back?” Phainon accused, dramatic as ever.


“No? We just talked like usual, right, Khas?” Mydei said, smirking proudly like he just won a competition.

Khaslana clapped his hands and flung himself into Mydei’s arms again, repeating “Dada! Dada!” like a war cry, soft and delighted.


“I swaddled you,” Phainon whispered to the child, eyes glistening. “I stayed up all night researching syllables. I bribed you with pear purée—pear, your favorite!”


Mydei reached out with his free hand, tugged Phainon closer and kissed his cheek. “Don’t pout. He’ll say your name soon. Probably when you’re elbow-deep in mashed pumpkin.”


Still, Phainon leaned down to kiss Khaslana’s tiny forehead. “I love you, even if you betrayed me with your first word,” he whispered. “But next one better be Papa.”


Khaslana giggled and smacked a spoon onto the floor. "Poon!"


“Or... ‘spoon,’ sure,” Phainon muttered, resigned.


And though he sulked for the rest of the afternoon, he still smiled when he thought no one was looking, especially when he saw Khaslana nestled in Mydei’s arms, sleepy and warm, whispering a soft “Dada” in his dreams.


Kremnos filled with celebration, everyone watched its young prince grow up beneath the sharp gaze of the sun and the gentler light of his parents’ love.


Each birthday had become a festival. Festive decorations were filling the town, petals rained from balconies, and bards were singing their praises. The people loved Khaslana, their little prince of quiet grace. But no one adored him more than the two people who had once bled for a future they could not even imagine and now found it nestled in the crook of their arms.


At five years old, Khaslana walked with a posture far too dignified for his size. He was a mirror of Mydei, stoic, sharp-eyed, always watching. His words were few but precise, his judgment swift and often devastating. Especially for Phainon.


The boy now called Mydei “Dad,” in a tone as solemn as a court announcement.


Phainon, on the other hand… “Papa,” drawn out with just the barest edge of exasperation, as though his very title came with chaos attached.


“You look tired, Papa,” Khaslana observed one morning, watching as Phainon stumbled into the breakfast room, eyes half-lidded.


“I was up at dawn preparing your favorite porridge!” Phainon whined.


“It's salty. I like Dad's cooking better.”


Phainon gasped, clutching his chest. “Protesting than thanking me? I raised you with these hands!”


Khaslana blinked. “Dad helped you. Also, Grandma and Lady Tribios.”


“You weren’t even supposed to know that!”


From his seat at the table, Mydei sipped his tea without looking up. “He read it in the royal archives.”


The boy nodded solemnly. “I read the parts where Papa fell off his horse twice when trying to win a hunter festival. You lost against Dad. It's fun..khm, a good lesson.”


“Ptolemy wrote that down?!”


“Very detailed,” Mydeimos said dryly.


Phainon groaned and slumped over the table, his son staring at him with that same unimpressed squint that Mydei often used.


But beneath the dry wit and the cold gleam in his gaze, Khaslana was still a child.


That afternoon, he’d been playing in the garden. Mydei nearby, reading on a bench, watching out of the corner of his eye when he tripped over a tree root and fell hard onto the gravel.


There was a sharp hiss from him. But then nothing.


He sat up quickly, brushing the dirt off, lips tight, small hands clenched on his scraped knee.


Mydei was already kneeling beside him before he could hide the forming tears.


“I’m fine,” Khaslana muttered, eyes focused elsewhere.


Mydei said nothing at first. Just gently wrapped an arm around the boy and sat down beside him on the grass. The breeze moved through the tree above, soft petals drifting down around them like slow snowfall.


“Does it hurt?” Mydei asked softly.


“...A little,” Khaslana admitted.


“It’s alright to say so.”


“I don’t want to cry.”


“Why not?”


“Because I want to be strong like you.”


That brought a frown to Mydei’s expression. He looked at his son then, at the small furrow between his brows, the trembling lip held with too much pride, the way he refused to meet his father’s gaze.


He reached over and brushed back a stray curl from Khaslana’s cheek.


“You know, I’ve cried many times,” Mydei said.


Khaslana blinked up. “You have?”


“Many. More than I can count. I’ve cried from fear, from pain, from anger, from love. And I don’t think it made me any less strong. In fact, it’s because I let myself feel those things that I became strong enough to carry them.”


The boy was silent.


“You’re allowed to cry, Khas. You don’t need to hide your pain to be worthy. Especially not from me. Or your papa.”


“But you never cry in front of anyone.”


Mydei gave a small smile. “That doesn’t mean I don’t cry. I just prefer to do it when your papa’s holding me.”


From behind a nearby hedge, Phainon’s voice cried out: “Am I supposed to pretend I didn’t hear that?!”


Khaslana blinked.


"Papa is there..."


“I’m telling you, your Papa will teleports when he hears his name called,” Mydei chuckled, standing and gently scooping the boy into his arms.


By the time they reached the bench, Phainon was already there. “What happened?! Are you hurt?! Is that blood?!”


Khaslana pointed to his knee. “It’s a scrape, Papa.”


“A SCRA—”


“Papa,” Mydei warned.


Phainon blinked, then adjusted his volume. “...Okay. Just a scrape.”


Mydei set Khaslana down and gently cleaned the wound, wrapping it with linen. Meanwhile, Phainon sat beside him, looking far more wounded than either of them.


“You’re not a porcelain doll, Khas, I know that,” Phainon said. “But still, I don’t like it when you hide things from us. It's okay to admit you need help, or when you're hurting.”


“I didn’t mean to hide it,” the boy murmured.


"I know. But wounds might get dangerous if being left alone." Mydei tilted his head. “And remember this: you don’t need to be perfect. You’re already loved.”


Khaslana glanced at him, then at Phainon, then finally gave the tiniest nod.


“...Then I want to cry now,” he whispered. "It hurts..."


Without a word, Mydei wrapped his arms around his son. Phainon joined in, pulling both of them into a warm, awkward tangle of limbs.


Khaslana sniffled quietly, hiding his face in Mydei’s chest.


“...I still think Papa is too loud,” he said between hiccups.


“I'm passionate,” Phainon corrected.


“Dad is cooler,” Khaslana added.


“I heard that and I agree,” Phainon replied, placing a kiss on the boy’s hair. Mydei chuckled, ruffling the identical silvery hairs in both hands.


Khaslana’s sniffles slowed. His arms wrapped a bit tighter around both of them. “But I love you both,” he whispered.


The spring wind passed softly through the garden, rustling the leaves above them as the small family caught in a perfect pocket of time.


In the royal chamber, the scent of myrtles clung to the air. A tray of half-eaten fruit and two untouched goblets of wine sat forgotten on the low table.


Phainon lay stretched beside Mydei, propped up on one elbow, watching him fondly. Mydei had gone quiet, not from exhaustion but from thought. He reclined against the headboard, a silk robe loose around his frame, chest bared, the candlelight flickering along the faint line of his collarbone. His golden eyes stared through the canopy, distant.


Phainon tilted his head. “You’re making that face again.”


“What face?”


“The face that says Khaslana just said something so profound it unsettled your soul.”


Mydei blinked, turned to him, and smirked faintly. “Close.”


Phainon’s grin widened. “What did our little philosopher say this time? Has he declared himself king of jam again?”


Mydei exhaled, amusement laced with something deeper. “He asked ‘If it’s okay to want something just because it makes you feel safe.’”


“That's... deep."


“I know.” Mydei glanced down, brows furrowed. “He said it when I told him it was okay to ask for help, even if he thought he didn’t need it. Then he went quiet for a while. Then asked that.”

Phainon then sat up fully now, crossing his legs, one hand coming to rest on Mydei’s thigh. “What did you say?”


“I told him yes. That even I have done the same.” He looked away, voice softening. “That sometimes, choosing safety doesn’t make you weak. It makes you wise.”

"What did he want, though?"

"A dromas as pet."

"...That's definitely influence from Professor Anaxa."

"Right. Definitely not kind of safety I initially thought."


They chuckled softly.

"Will you grant his wish, though?"

"No. I said that not every wish would come true so easily. Somehow, one had to do everything to gain it. So, I told him to study harder and prove me that he could take care a dromas before I let him adopt one."


Phainon reached up, gently tracing his thumb along Mydei’s cheekbone. “You are such a good father.”

"I wonder if I really am..."

" Well, Khas already made you his role model. That means he knows you're a good father."


Mydei closed his eyes, leaning to the gentle touch. “He’s five. He still thinks I invented war.”


Phainon leaned in, their foreheads touching. “Doesn’t mean you haven’t already shaped him into someone better.”


Their breaths mingled. Mydei let his hand trail up Phainon’s arm, slow, deliberate. “You're the one who taught him to name his feelings.”


“And you're the one who showed him it's okay to have them.”

Their lips met, no rush, no demand. Just warmth.


It deepened gradually, like flame coaxed to life. Mydei’s fingers curled in Phainon’s shirt, tugging him closer. Phainon let out a breath, part surprised, part aching, and slid his hand down to Mydei’s waist, thumb grazing the edge of exposed skin where the robe had fallen open.


Their mouths found rhythm, familiar and intimate. Mydei shifted, guiding Phainon between his legs, silk parting around them. The warmth between their bodies built like a rising tide, slow and steady, sinking into their bones.


Phainon kissed down Mydei’s throat, letting his lips linger there. He moved lower, reverent as a worshipper, until he reached the swell of Mydei’s chest, pressing his mouth to the soft skin with a breathless sound.


“I missed you,” he murmured.


“I noticed,” Mydei said, a smirk curling as his fingers threaded through Phainon’s hair. "Well, it had been like, what, three weeks?"


“Yeah, three weeks but it feels like a long time already. I missed holding you every single night without anyone intruding. And somehow, you feel different each time,” Phainon said quietly, sliding his hand across Mydei’s hip. “Softer. Warmer.”


“I’m still me.”


“I know.” Phainon’s eyes met his, the blue deepening. “That’s what makes it unbearable.”


He leaned in again, this time kissing the corner of Mydei’s lips, his jaw, down his neck. His hand found the dip of Mydei’s back, drawing him forward. The air around them grew heavier, charged with want wrapped in familiarity. Their robes slipped further. Skin touched skin. Nothing frantic, only hunger that knew its name.


Phainon kissed the swell of Mydei’s chest again, then lower, tongue tasting the skin just above his navel. There was no mark from the surgery, it healed so fast like his other wounds. However, the rite marking was branded on his skin like a permanent scar. Phainon sighed softly, starting to rain down the kisses all around the toned stomach which once carried his child.


“You’re making a habit of worshipping,” Mydei teased, strained with breath catching with every touch.


“I’ve had years of practice,” Phainon murmured. “Might as well show off.”


Their bodies pressed together again, and Mydei arched up into him, a sharp intake of breath escaping his lips. The slide of Phainon’s palm along his thigh was slow, as though he were carving every second into memory.


Then—


Knock. Knock.


They both froze.


Phainon blinked, lips still barely brushing Mydei’s skin. “Tell me that was your stomach.”


Mydei stared toward the door, disbelief painting his features. “Don't be denial now.”


Knock. Knock. Knock.


Phainon groaned into the pillow and slowly peeled himself off his husband, dragging a robe over his half-draped form like a martyr ascending the gallows.


“If this is about raisins—”


Mydei reclined back, adjusting his robe without urgency. “I warned you. You gave him sugar after dinner.”


“I regret everything,” Phainon muttered as he reached the door, rubbing a hand over his flushed face.


The door creaked open.


A small voice piped up, holding up a purple stuffed doll. “Papa, I think my dromas is scared of the dark. Can he sleep in your bed?”


Phainon smiled at Khaslana but the smile disappeared once he turned to look at Mydei.


“He brought the whole army.”


Mydei chuckled, already sitting upright and adjusting the sheets. “Well, better make room. Your tyrant has arrived.”


"Right. Come in, Khas."


Phainon shuffled back into bed, defeated, and face-planted beside him.


“We were so close.”


Mydei snorted softly and kissed the top of his head. “Tomorrow night.”


Phainon groaned again. “You always say that.”


“But you always fall for it.”


“Because I’m stupid.”


“Because you’re in love,” Mydei corrected, stroking his hair.


And Khaslana marched with doll in tow and a blanket that trailed behind him like a royal mantle, ready to conquer the peace of another night. He had clambered up and made himself comfortable between his fathers, claiming the center of the universe, as was his birthright.


He yawned, squirmed under the covers, and then turned on his side to face Mydei, tiny hand patting gently over the smooth plane of Mydei’s stomach.


“Papa shouldn’t bully Dad too much,” he mumbled gravely, eyelids heavy. “It’ll scare my little sister.”


Mydei blinked. Phainon slowly turned his head from where he lay slumped, still recovering from the failed seduction attempt.


“...Your what now?” Phainon asked. "You, want a little sibling?"


Khaslana shook his head solemnly, his fingers still resting on Mydei’s stomach as if in protection. “No, my sister is already in here.”


The air changed.


Phainon scrambled upright like a startled cat, covers flying off. “Perdikkas. I’m calling Perdikkas.” And he dashed out the room.


Khaslana blinked at him from his nest of blankets. “Is Papa okay?”


“He’s just... very happy,” Mydei said gently, amusement passed behind his golden eyes. “Did you see your little sister?”


Khaslana shook his head again, snuggling in closer to Mydei’s side, as if drawn to a warmth only he could feel.


“I saw Grandma,” he whispered.


Mydei’s hand froze for a fraction of a second where it stroked Khaslana’s hair. “Grandma?”


Khaslana looked up, brow wrinkling slightly. “Not the one from Aedes Elysiae. The other one. She smiled a lot. She said she’s happy you’re happy now.” He paused, thoughtful. “She told me about my sister too. She said Dad has my sister in his tummy now.”


The words weren’t spoken with eerie certainty, or dramatic flair. Just the innocent conviction only children possessed, like truth drawn from somewhere older than language.


Mydei’s breath left him slow and silent. He looked down at his son, whose lashes had already begun to flutter with sleep. He pulled Khaslana closer, his arm wrapping around the small, warm body nestled to his side.


"...I see,” he murmured, almost to himself.


Mydei held his son tightly and closed his eyes. He hummed something low under his breath, lulling Khaslana to sleep, hand still stroking his hair.


And across the room, Phainon returned in a half-panicked daze.


“…Did he fall asleep?”


Mydei nodded, murmured softer than the night breeze. “And he brought a miracle with him.”


Phainon stared at them, his husband, his son, and perhaps something more. His breath caught in his chest, unsure whether to laugh or weep.


“Perdikkas is coming here.”


"Let's waiting in silence, then."


Phainon nodded solemnly and tiptoed closer with the exaggerated caution of someone defusing a bomb.


Mydei looked down again at Khaslana, fingers resting lightly where the child’s hand had touched moments before. And though he said nothing, a smile played at the corner of his lips, a secret known only to parents, and perhaps to those who dreamed the flower field.


The banners of Kremnos still cast long shadows across Amphoreus, but they no longer a storm that tore the calm. The kingdom was no less powerful, its might was legendary, its armies unmatched. But now, it was not fear that made other nations bow. It was respect. Kremnos had become a nation of balance, of justice and order, where might served peace, and allowed its people to thrive. Even the oldest enemies had learned that a blade tempered by mercy cut cleaner than one soaked in cruelty.


The seasons changed, and spring settled over the kingdom like a soft shawl. The sun filtered through the stained glass of the castle’s halls, spilling color onto polished floors. Flowers bloomed on every sill, and the scent of cakes drifted faintly from the kitchens.


Down one corridor padded Khaslana, a boy of ten now, proud, sharp-eyed, dressed in a kremnoan's traditional garb for a casual stroll. His steps were light, but sure. His golden eyes held a strange quiet wisdom for someone so young, though he still bore the glint of mischief.


He turned a corner, glanced both ways, then stopped before the tall double doors of his parents' chamber. They were slightly ajar.


He slipped inside, silent as a breeze.


The bed was made, the papers stacked neatly on the desk. Empty.


Khaslana, however, walked straight to the towering wardrobe at the far end. He tugged one door open with both hands, careful not to let it creak.


Nestled in a makeshift fort of cloaks and robes, a small girl sat cross-legged on the floor, a stuffed chimera clutched tightly to her chest.


“Gorgo,” Khaslana said, folding his arms.


The little girl blinked up at him. Her golden-blond hair was tousled by her hiding, her blue eyes shimmering with guilt. “I’m not here,” she declared.


Khaslana stepped inside the wardrobe and crouched down. “Lady Castorice has been looking for you all afternoon.”


Gorgo pouted, hugging her chimera tighter. “I don’t want to come out.”


“You’ve missed your lessons.”


“I know,” she sniffled. “But I made a mistake.”


“A mistake?” he echoed, raising an eyebrow.


Gorgo nodded solemnly. “I dropped the ink all over the pretty map. It had all the sea monsters drawn and everything. And then I tried to clean it with the towel and it got worse. Lady Castorice gasped like this,” She opened her mouth dramatically in a silent ‘oh’, “and then I ran.”


Khaslana leaned his elbow on one bent knee, resting his chin on his palm. “So you thought hiding in the wardrobe until the sun exploded was a good plan?”


“...Yes.”


He chuckled. “Gorgo.”


She looked up at him, lower lip quivering. “You’re not going to tell Dad, are you?”


“Why wouldn’t I?” he asked mildly. “You ruined his map.”


Her eyes widened in horror. “Khas!”


He grinned, unable to hold back a laugh, then softened. “No one’s going to be angry, Gorgo. It was a mistake.”


“But you never make mistakes,” she mumbled. “You always do everything right. Papa says you’re perfect.”


Khaslana blinked. “I think Papa might need to get his eyes checked.”


She still looked skeptical.


He leaned closer, lowering his voice like he was telling her a great secret. “Did I ever tell you how I once sent a diplomatic pigeon with the wrong letter to the King of Aidonia?”


Gorgo gasped. “You didn’t.”


“I did. I sent the one where I drew Dad and Papa fighting sea monsters and wrote ‘Our kingdom will devour yours, RAWR.’”


Her hands flew to her mouth, eyes wide.


“I cried for an hour,” Khaslana admitted. “Papa panicked and Dad had to write three more letters to fix it. And they still didn’t get angry.”


Gorgo’s brow furrowed. “But I'm not you. You’re smart. You read all those big books and you speak three languages.”


He shrugged. “And I still do dumb things sometimes. That’s how you learn. Besides...” He reached out and gently brushed a leaf from her hair. “It’s braver to come out and say ‘I made a mistake’ than to never make one at all.”


“...You’re just saying that because Papa says it.”


“And Papa’s very smart... Although, I hate to admit it,” Khaslana replied, helping her up from the pile of cloaks. “Now come on. We’ll apologize together."


Gorgo nodded and slipped her hand into his. The two young royals walked down the hall back to the study room.


In the room, warm afternoon light filtered through the high windows. The table had been cleared of most documents, save for one unfortunate map still drying its stain. Mydei and Phainon stood near the desk, having only just returned from their meeting. Castorice stood to the side, arms gently folded, smiling gently.


As soon as they entered, Gorgo froze behind her brother, fingers digging into the fabric of his tunic. Her eyes were wide, shimmering with unshed tears, as if hiding behind Khaslana could undo everything.


Khaslana gave her hand a gentle tug. “It’s okay,” he whispered, nudging her forward.


Gorgo stepped out slowly, eyes downcast, until she stood before Castorice. She gave a tiny bow. “I’m sorry for making you worry, Lady Castorice.”


Castorice smiled. “It's okay, Princess. I’m just glad you’re safe.”


Then, Gorgo turned to Mydei, her fingers still clutching tightly to her brother’s. “I... I’m sorry for ruining the map, Dad.”


Mydei didn’t speak right away. He stepped forward, lowering himself into a crouch so that his golden eyes met hers, steady but kind. “Thank you for apologizing,” he said. “The map can be redrawn. But next time, don’t hide away. That was what worried us.”


Gorgo’s lip quivered. “I thought you’d be angry and then you will hate me…”


Mydei gently touched her cheek. “Making mistakes doesn’t mean we’ll stop loving you, Gorgo.”

"Really...?"

"Yes, I'm proud that you owned your mistake. Thank you for being honest with us."


At that, she broke into tears, soft and stifled, and threw herself into his arms. He held her close, rubbing her back as her little shoulders shook, and across the room, Phainon nodded with a proud, if slightly misty, grin.


“Well then,” Phainon clapped his hands. “We’ve earned a break. Cookies, cakes, and hot tea await in the garden. And yes,” he added with a wink to Gorgo, “your favorite orange scones too.”


Gorgo sniffled, eyes lighting up. “Really?”


“Would your Papa lie?”


“Frequently,” Khaslana said, with unspoken grudge.


Phainon gasped, clutching his chest like wounded nobility. “Traitor!”


They all laughed, even Gorgo through her remaining tears. Mydei extended a hand toward Castorice. “You’ll join us, I hope?”


But Castorice shook her head. “I’d love to, but I have an appointment with Hyacine and Dan Heng.” She bowed slightly. “Enjoy your tea, Your Majesties.”


And with that, she slipped away, leaving the family alone.


They made their way to the balcony where a low table had already been prepared. The warm spring breeze stirred the gauzy curtains, and the scent of honeyed cakes mingled with blooming jasmine.


Gorgo nestled beside Mydei, her head against his side. Khaslana sat at the opposite side, sipping his tea like a diplomat in training. Phainon, of course, plopped himself down with unrefinedly and immediately stole a bite from Mydei’s plate.


As Gorgo nibbled on a scone, cheeks still a little pink from her earlier tears, Phainon leaned his head against Mydei’s shoulder and sighed contentedly.


“You know,” he said softly, “you were so worried you wouldn’t be a good father.”


Mydei turned slightly, brushing his fingers through Gorgo’s hair. “That’s because I didn’t know what kind of father I’d be.”


“And now?”


Mydei looked at him. “Now I know, I’m good at it because I’m not doing it alone.”


Phainon smiled. He leaned in and kissed Mydei gently, a soft brush of lips laced with years of devotion.


“Hey!” Gorgo cried, “That’s not fair! I want a kiss too!”

"Say no less! Here come a kiss for you!"


So, Phainon kissed Gorgo, a loud, squelchy smooch on the cheek.


She squealed with joy, hugging her father back. “Papa! You're tickling me!”


Phainon beamed, ruffling her hair. “That’s payment for being the cutest creature in this entire kingdom.”


He then turned toward Khaslana, narrowing his eyes in challenge. “Well? Shall I give you one too?”


Khaslana raised his chin. “Absolutely not,” he said. “I’m trying to finish my tea in peace.”


Phainon gasped. “Wow, my son is too prideful for a kiss now.”


Mydei bit back a snort.


“I have matured, Papa.” Khaslana added, his voice unwavering. “Please respect my boundaries.”


“Do you even know what boundaries meant?”


"Of course. Professor Anaxagoras taught me everything."


Mydei tilted his head. “Then what if I want to give you one, Khas? Should I stop too?”


Khaslana hesitated. His cheek twitched. Then, with just the slightest bob of his head, he nodded. "If it's Dad, It's okay..."


Phainon immediately launched himself across the seat to smother him in kisses. “You little traitor! You’d take his kiss but not mine?!”


Khaslana shrieked, for once breaking his composure as he tried to wriggle away. “Papa, you’re—ugh! Stop!”


“I loved you first!” Phainon howled. “I changed your diapers! I cleaned your snot!”


“I didn’t ask you to! Stop messing my hair!"

“You declared war first!” Phainon declared playfully. “You said you didn’t want my kiss but then tried to steal my husband’s! I will not be defeated by a child with good posture!”

“I'll challenge you in colosseum then I’ll marry Dad when I grow up!” Khaslana stated, pushing back with a defiant snort.

Phainon recoiled, jaw dropping. “What?! That’s treason! You little—!”


Gorgo clapped, grinning with all her teeth on display. “They’re fighting again!”


Mydei shook his head slowly and looked up at the sky, the colors warm and soft above the kingdom that had once been steeped in crimson.


He used to avoid looking too far into the sky, afraid it might remind him of the past. Of a small, trembling boy running barefoot through pain, of fear that chased him down, of a mother’s warmth vanishing from his memory.


But now?


He looked up and smiled.


No longer did his heart carry the guilt of surviving. He understood now, fully, achingly: her final act was love, not sacrifice. She had not simply died for him. She had lived her last breath for his life. And that life now bloomed with laughter, peace, and a love that held no sharp edges.


He owed her everything.


And he had everything, thanks to his husband.

Phainon, who once walked through loneliness just to reach him, who made the cold halls warm with wild flowers, who kissed every wound to ease, he had given him this gentle world, brick by brick, promise by promise.


There were days Mydei doubted he deserved such peace.


But every time Phainon looked at him like he was the light that taught the sun how to shine, every time their children laughed, every time the halls echoed with love instead of commands, he decided to believe a little more.


“Enough,” he said finally, reaching out to seize both father and son by the collars as they play-wrestled on the grass, tangled in a sea of limbs and mock protests.


Gorgo giggled again. Khaslana huffed and stood up straight. Then, Mydei kissed his son gently on the forehead. “You two are just too much,” he said fondly.


Phainon pouted. “Hey, what about me?”


With a chuckle, Mydei leaned in and brushed a kiss against his lips, slower, softer.


His fingers touched Phainon’s cheek as he whispered, “I love you. For all that you are. For all that you’ve given me.”


Phainon flushed deep, speechless for a rare moment.


Khaslana groaned and covered Gorgo’s eyes. “Not in front of the us, please?”


Gorgo giggled again. “Dad and Papa are kissing!”


And as the golden afternoon passed into evening, as the family nestled closer for another shared tale, another plate of sweets, another round of laughter. The world outside Kremnos could only wonder what made the mighty kingdom so unshakably strong.


The answer was this: a kiss, a promise kept, and the love that stitched it all together.
